card.hook: Edinburgh Castle looks like the walls grew straight out of the rock, and that's because the rock is an extinct volcano from roughly 350 million years ago. Your phone loves it.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 120 m north-west of the subject, and face south-east. From here the rock and the walls sit together in one frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole castle and rock in. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the walls and towers. Use 0.5x only if you want lots of foreground or sky, because it makes the castle look small and far away.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the castle walls, then slide it a little darker if the sky is bright so the stonework keeps its detail (or a little brighter on a grey day).
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives soft light that flatters the stonework. After dark, switch on night mode and rest your phone against a wall or railing to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Ross Fountain in Princes Street Gardens West, where the castle rises directly behind it. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold it low so the castle towers over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: On the Castle Esplanade, stand in front of the castle façade and ask someone to step back so they can frame the whole fortress with you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is allowed in most of the castle, but flash is not. Check the official castle pages before you visit, and note that going inside is likely to need a ticket.
card.challenge: Take one shot at 1x and one zoomed in, then see if you can guess which one your friends will 'like' more.
card.good_to_know: Castle Rock is about 130 metres above sea level, with cliffs on the south, west and north dropping around 80 metres. A royal castle has stood here since the 11th century, and a 2014 count found 26 sieges in its 1,100-year history. St Margaret's Chapel, from the early 12th century, is regarded as the oldest building in Edinburgh.

card.hook: There's a whole extinct volcano parked about a mile east of Edinburgh Castle, and it's sitting there like it owns the place. Fair enough, it's been here a few hundred million years.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 1.1 km north-west of Arthur's Seat and the Salisbury Crags, and face south-east. The hill stays in view ahead of you the whole way.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the hill sits in its surroundings. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the crags and the summit. Skip 0.5x here, because it makes the hill look small and far away.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the top of the hill on the upper third line, then tap the crags and slide the brightness down a touch so the sky keeps its colour and the rock stays dark and textured.
card.best_time: Late afternoon or evening is usually best, when low sun falls on the crags. Clear days after rain give the sharpest view.
card.selfie_here: Climb the grassy paths up Salisbury Crags (not the Radical Road) and stand above the cliff edge with Arthur's Seat's summit directly behind you. Or go to the top, beside the white Ordnance Survey pillar, and make the city and Forth views your backdrop. Use the front camera, hold it a little low, and keep the landmark over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Rock climbing on the crags has been banned since 2019 and the Radical Road path has been closed since 2018, so check the official site for current access. It can get really windy at the summit because it's close to the coast, so take care up there.
card.challenge: Squint at the hill from your spot and see if you can find the lion lying down, then get it in your shot.
card.good_to_know: Arthur's Seat is an extinct volcano that rises to 250.5 m (822 ft) in Holyrood Park. The lava is roughly 341 to 335 million years old, and a glacier later scraped away the western side to leave the Salisbury Crags. Two of its old volcanic vents are called the Lion's Head and the Lion's Haunch.

selfie_spots.why: A guide describes the summit being directly at your back from the Crags, with the basalt cliffs in front for a dramatic frame.

card.hook: The Royal Mile squeezes you between tall old tenements while the street tips gently downhill, and you will never get it to yourself. So don't fight the crowds. Use them to show how big everything is.
card.stand_here: On the Royal Mile, stand about 25 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. You're looking up the slope with the buildings on both sides leading your eye along the street.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the full height of the buildings and the sweep of the street. Switch to 1x for natural-looking street scenes, then try 2x to pick out rooftops, chimneys and signs.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the tall building edges with the vertical lines so they don't lean, then tap the sky and slide it a little darker so it doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning for the fewest people in your shot. It gets crowded later in the day, and especially during the Edinburgh Fringe. In the evening, switch on night mode and rest your phone against a wall or railing to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Camera Obscura & World of Illusions rooftop terrace on Castlehill, beside Edinburgh Castle. It looks straight along the Royal Mile, so use the front camera (try 0.5x) and let the street stretch out behind your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: For a photo of you with the whole view, ask a passer-by at the lookout next to Nelson's Monument on Calton Hill to snap you with Arthur's Seat, the Salisbury Crags and the Royal Mile all behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks aren't allowed inside the Edinburgh Castle precinct, but a phone is fine. The Calton Hill route from the High Street involves some steep hills, so wear comfy shoes.
card.challenge: Find a close (a narrow alleyway) opening off the street and tuck it into the edge of your frame, then see if a stranger walks past for a bit of scale.
card.good_to_know: The Royal Mile is really a chain of streets running from Edinburgh Castle down to Holyrood Palace, and it's almost exactly one mile long. The street drops from about 109 m above sea level at the castle to about 42 m at the palace. Much of the south side of the High Street was rebuilt or refaced in a Georgian style after the Great Edinburgh Fire of 1824.

card.hook: Walk to the very bottom of the Royal Mile and you hit a palace with a castle-style tower and a ruined abbey next to it. It's the King's official home in Scotland, and it's a lot less crowded than the castle at the other end.
card.stand_here: Stand about 150 m west of the Palace of Holyroodhouse, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. James V's Tower will be on the left, at the north-west corner.
card.zoom: Start at 1x and step back a bit so the whole front fits with some sky above. Then try 2x for the tower and windows. Save 0.5x for a close-up of the gates or the ground in front, because it makes the palace look small and far away from here.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the base of the palace on the lower line, then tap the palace and drag the slider down a touch to make it darker if the sky is bright.
card.best_time: Late afternoon or early evening is a good bet, because the sun should be shining on the west front. Go early in the day if you want fewer people in your shot.
card.selfie_here: Head onto the forecourt by the fountain, inside the wrought-iron gates, so the palace front is behind you and the Royal Mile view is ahead. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to squeeze more in, and hold the phone a little lower so the palace sits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the small rise just inside the Holyrood Park gates, looking back across Abbey Strand toward the palace, while you pose with the palace behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Inside the palace, selfie sticks, flash and stabilisers are off-limits. That's the rule we found for inside only, so check the official site before you go in.
card.challenge: Spot James V's Tower, the big one with rounded corners, and get one shot with it neatly framed and the walls standing straight up.
card.good_to_know: The oldest surviving part of the palace is James V's Tower, built between 1528 and 1536. The abbey beside it was founded in 1128, and James IV began building a Gothic palace next to it in 1501. Mary, Queen of Scots lived in the tower's apartments in the 1560s.

card.hook: The Royal Mile is a squeeze of narrow, busy streets, and right in the middle of it sits a dark, carved-stone church that looks like it's been watching the crowds forever. That's St Giles', and it's one of the easiest places in Edinburgh to photograph.
card.stand_here: Head to the High Street section of the Royal Mile and stand at the phone icon, about 25 m north-east of the cathedral. Face south-west and look across the street at the building, so you can fit more in than you could from right beside the walls.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole building as people see it from the street. If the street is too tight to fit the tower and walls in, tap 0.5x. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the stonework and the top of the tower.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the tower up with one vertical line so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Expect people in your shots at most times of day, so use them to show how big the building is, or wait a moment for a gap. If people keep walking through, try a Live Photo and pick the best frame afterwards.
card.selfie_here: Try the Heart of Midlothian mosaic on the cobbles beside the cathedral, where visitors already stop for pictures. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if you need more room, and shuffle around until the stonework sits over your shoulder. For something quieter, the carved wooden gates of the back door, across from the City Chambers, put the cathedral's own stonework behind you.
card.ask_someone: In Parliament Square, stand among the statues and ask your passer-by to stand back across the square so the cathedral's crown spire fills the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Personal photos are allowed inside, but not of other visitors, staff or volunteers. There's no photography during services, no flash, and some sections restrict photos altogether. It's an active church, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Catch the tower dead straight on a gridline with a bit of Royal Mile street in the foreground, then step closer and grab one close-up of the carved stone.
card.good_to_know: The church you see today was begun in the 14th century and extended until the early 16th century. The Thistle Chapel was added between 1909 and 1911. John Knox was its minister after the Scottish Reformation, and the cathedral had over a million visitors in 2018.

card.hook: Everyone climbs Calton Hill for the view. Here's a plan with a twist: stand back and photograph the hill itself, crowded with monuments, with the Scott Monument and the Old Town in front.
card.stand_here: Head for the Mound in Princes Street Gardens, the slope between the east and west gardens, and stand about 1.2 km south-west of the subject (that's the phone icon on the map). Face north-east and Calton Hill is there in the distance.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the Scott Monument, the Old Town and the hill in one wide shot. Then try zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to bring the hill closer so its monuments are easier to see.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the hill on one of the upper thirds and keep the phone level so the skyline doesn't tilt.
card.best_time: One photo-spot guide suggests sunrise for this view. Check the sunrise time for your date and arrive a little early to find your spot.
card.selfie_here: Climb up and use the front camera on the steps of the National Monument, with its unfinished Doric columns behind you (Hotels.com recommends the steps for photos). Want fewer people? Try beside the Dugald Stewart Monument, away from the main path, though the view there is a little lower.
card.ask_someone: At the Dugald Stewart Monument, ask a passer-by to come up the Waterloo Place steps on the summit path side and take your photo with the whole monument in frame.
card.rules_and_safety: In winter the slopes can be muddy and slippery, roughly a 40-degree incline, so take care on the grassy banks. Check the official site for opening times, closures and events before you go.
card.challenge: Zoom in on the hill and count how many monuments you can spot on its skyline, then see if your friends get the same number.
card.good_to_know: Calton Hill is part of Edinburgh's UNESCO World Heritage Site, and its monuments include the National Monument, the Nelson Monument and the old Royal High School. In 1787 the artist Robert Barker was inspired by walking here and created the world's first panorama. It was a 360-degree view of Edinburgh painted from the City Observatory tower.

card.hook: Walk down the steep slope from the West End and the traffic noise just drops away. Suddenly you're in a quiet stone village by a river, with a huge bridge far above you.
card.stand_here: Stand at the bottom of Hawthornbank Lane, by the river, about 95 m south-east of the subject, where steps lead down to the water. Face north-west and look across the river to Well Court and the stone houses.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the houses, river and bridge into one shot. If you're close to the water and it feels tight, tap 0.5x. Try 2x to pick out Well Court's details (higher zooms depend on your phone), so you don't have to lean over the water.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the stonework, then slide the picture a little darker so the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning or late in the afternoon, when the light is softest. A still day gives you the best reflections in the water.
card.selfie_here: Try the small footbridge over the river in the village, with the historic stone arch behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold it a little low so the arch fills the background over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to take your photo from Bell's Brae Bridge, at the top of Bell's Brae, looking upstream along the river.
card.rules_and_safety: People live here, so keep your voice down, stay off doorsteps and keep drones at home. Well Court's courtyard is private, so shoot it from outside the gate. Watch your footing on the cobbles and the uneven path at water level.
card.challenge: On a still day, try to get the houses and their reflection in one shot. A Live Photo might even catch a ripple, so wait for the calmest moment.
card.good_to_know: For more than 800 years, Dean Village was a grain-milling community on the Water of Leith, and at one time it had eleven working mills. Today the old mills and cottages are homes. High above, Thomas Telford's Dean Bridge was built in 1831-2 and opened in 1833. It stands 106 feet above the water.

card.hook: Picture Victorian stonework right next to you, the city's rooftops spread out beyond it, and not a single street-level lamppost in the way. That's the idea up on the National Museum of Scotland's roof terrace, though you'll want to check it's open first.
card.stand_here: Stand about 30 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. Then turn around to take in the wider view from the same spot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit in the roofline and the sweep of the city. Switch to 1x for a natural view, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out distant rooftops, spires and stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines to keep the horizon level, then tap the brightest part of the sky and slide darker a touch so the clouds don't wash out.
card.best_time: Pick a dry, clear day when the terrace is open. Early morning or late afternoon usually means softer light and fewer people in your shot.
card.selfie_here: Stand beside the four orange sandstone blocks by Andy Goldsworthy on the terrace, so the terrace stays in your frame. For a skyline selfie, go to the terrace edge and face north, so the crown spire of St Giles' Cathedral sits behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold it a little low so the landmark peeks over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Roof terrace access and arrangements aren't confirmed here, so check the official museum site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot and one close-up from the same spot, then see if you can get a chimney or roof edge in the foreground of the wide one.
card.good_to_know: The museum is two connected buildings on Chambers Street. The Victorian one was begun in 1861 and partly opened in 1866, with a Venetian Renaissance façade and a cast-iron central hall. The modern building opened in 1998, and the Royal Museum building reopened on 29 July 2011 after a three-year restoration. It's free to enter and was Scotland's most visited attraction in 2025, so expect other people in your frame.

card.hook: Edinburgh's Old Town skyline is packed with so much detail that you'll want to take your time over it. Luckily, your phone copes with all of it.
card.stand_here: Head to Waverley Bridge and stand about 80 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south.
card.zoom: Start at 1x with gridlines on, and line the horizon up with a gridline so the rooftops sit level. Want more skyline? Try 0.5x, but keep straight lines away from the edges, where they can lean. For one building or roofline, use 2x-5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of the buildings, then slide it darker a touch if the sky looks washed out.
card.best_time: Soft morning or evening light usually suits a skyline like this, and a clear day shows the rooftops best. At dusk, switch on night mode and brace your phone against something steady.
card.selfie_here: Try the bridge pavement at the Cockburn Street end, near the foot of Cockburn Street, where the Old Town rises above the station. Use the front camera at 0.5x and fit the skyline in over your shoulder. Guides rate this corner in golden hour light and on moody, cloudy or rainy days.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by at the green space reached from the corner of Princes Street and Waverley Bridge, where the Old Town view sits beyond.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working street area, so stay on the pavement and watch for traffic and other pedestrians. One guide advises against walking up to the Royal Mile from Waverley Bridge, because the ascent and stairs are steep.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot with a passer-by in the foreground, then one close-up of a single roofline, and see which one you like better.
card.good_to_know: This view is number 9 on our map. It works best as a scene-setter: the whole skyline with a little foreground, like passing people, to give a sense of place. Take a couple of frames, because the traffic and people change the scene from second to second.

card.hook: Years of city smoke have turned this Victorian tower dark and dramatic, so it looks moody even on a sunny day. The spire is so detailed that it works as a photo all by itself.
card.stand_here: Head into Princes Street Gardens and stand at the phone icon on the map, about 80 m west of the monument. Face east and the whole spire fits in with gardens and trees around it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x with your phone held upright to catch the full height. If people or trees crowd the edges, try 0.5x. For the carved figures and the top of the spire, use 2x to 5x if your phone has them.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the spire on a vertical line, and tap the dark stone, then drag it a little darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Early morning and the hour before sunset tend to give softer light. After dark, try night mode and rest your phone against a wall or railing to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Walk a few steps into Princes Street Gardens from the monument and use the greenery or flowers around you as a frame. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and tilt it up so the tower rises over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on the Princes Street pavement, opposite the former Jenners building, to shoot across the street looking east, so the monument is in the background.
card.rules_and_safety: The upper stairwells inside are extremely tight, so the climb isn't suited to anyone who is claustrophobic. The viewing platforms are a separate visit, so check the official site for access and tickets.
card.challenge: Can you spot the pointed pinnacles and arches, then zoom in on a few of the 64 carved figures without leaving the path?
card.good_to_know: The monument remembers the Scottish author Sir Walter Scott. The tower is 61.11 metres high and is made of Binny sandstone. Building finished in 1844 and it was inaugurated in 1846. Inside is a white marble statue of Scott with his dog Maida, and 287 steps lead to the highest viewing platform.

card.hook: Most people come for the little dog, then stop dead at the gate because the graveyard behind him is so packed: leaning headstones, domed tombs, carved wall monuments and a church, all squeezed into one patch.
card.stand_here: Head to Greyfriars Kirkyard and stand at the phone icon on the map, about 85 m east of the subject, and face west. You'll have the headstones in front of you and the Kirk behind them.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to get the whole scene of headstones with the Kirk behind. Use 1x for single monuments and the entrance, then 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for carved details on the wall monuments, so you never need to step off the paths.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and use the paths as lines leading into the picture, and keep the horizon level so the old stones don't look tipsy.
card.best_time: Soft, overcast light or early in the day suits stone and carving best. There are usually fewer people around then too.
card.selfie_here: Try the pavement in front of Greyfriars Kirk, a few yards to the left of the Bobby statue, so the church is behind you. One visitor review rates it better than posing at the statue itself, so use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and have a look when you arrive since there's no exact spot.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is permitted throughout the kirkyard. Keep to the paths, stay quiet near graves, and wait a moment for people to move out of your frame. Check the official site for current visiting arrangements, as the locked Covenanters' Prison section is only open by arrangement with the Kirk guides or on a tour.
card.challenge: Find a row of headstones with a path running past it and get the Kirk peeking out behind, with not a single stranger in the frame (good luck, and be patient).
card.good_to_know: Burials began in the 1560s, and the National Covenant was signed in the kirk in 1638. Early photographers David Octavius Hill and Robert Adamson used the graveyard as a setting for portraits in the 1840s. Bobby's headstone stands at the entrance, put up by the Dog Aid Society in 1981, and his statue is opposite the gate.

card.hook: The Grassmarket sits in a hollow, so Castle Rock seems to loom right over the pub roofs like it's nosing in on your lunch. It's one of those spots where the street and the skyline fit in one shot.
card.stand_here: Head for the phone icon on the map in the Grassmarket, about 110 m south-west of the subject. Face north-east and you'll get the whole street with the castle rock rising on one side.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole street and the rock above it. If the buildings feel cramped, try 0.5x. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out castle walls, rooflines or shop signs.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the buildings, then slide the brightness down a touch so the sky doesn't turn white.
card.best_time: Early morning is usually the quietest, so you can catch the street with hardly anyone in it. Late afternoon and evening usually bring warmer light and glowing pub windows, but expect more people.
card.selfie_here: Try the top landing of the Vennel steps, which run up from the west end of the Grassmarket. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x, and hold it low so the castle fits over your shoulder. Cold Town House's roof terrace at 4 Grassmarket is another option, open weather permitting.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the third step up from the bottom (not the landing) and shoot up the stair, with you posing on the steps above and the castle rising behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Stay on the pavement edges and keep clear of the road and any outdoor tables. The Vennel steps are steep, with no ramp or lift alternative.
card.challenge: Hunt down the inscribed flagstone in front of the White Hart Inn and get it in a shot with the castle rock above it.
card.good_to_know: The Grassmarket began as a market place, and from 1477 it was one of Edinburgh's main markets, with part of it used for selling horses and cattle. It was also a place of public executions, and a memorial from 1937 near the old gallows site remembers more than 100 Covenanters who died between 1661 and 1688. The flagstone by the White Hart Inn marks where a bomb fell during a Zeppelin raid in April 1916.

card.hook: Victoria Street rewards slow walkers: a splash of colour here, a bold shape there, and a stranger who strolls into your frame at exactly the right moment. Take your time and look up as well as ahead.
card.stand_here: On Victoria Street, stand about 40 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. Stand a little to one side so you're not in the way of people walking past.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view, and switch to 0.5x if you can't fit the whole scene in. Try 2x or more to pick out one detail that stands out.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines in your camera app and line a building edge up with a vertical line, so the street looks straight (and keep your phone level, as tilting up makes buildings lean).
card.best_time: Early morning is likely to be the quietest, with fewer people in your shot. Take a Live Photo too, so you can pick the moment the view is clear.
card.selfie_here: Head up to Victoria Terrace, the raised walkway above the street (stone steps at the lower end near the Grassmarket, or from George IV Bridge). It's an elevated spot where you may get a shot without vehicles or pedestrians in the way, but check the view before you stand. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the street behind your shoulder. For the full curve of the street, try the bottom corner at the foot of the West Bow, near the La Barantine cafe.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the top of the street near Howies at the George IV Bridge end, while you walk down the curve towards them.
card.rules_and_safety: Delivery and access vehicles still appear on the street, so keep half an eye on the road. Ask permission before photographing inside any shop or on private property.
card.challenge: Line a building edge up with a gridline, then wait for just one walker to step into the frame. Snap a few and pick your favourite!
card.good_to_know: Victoria Street runs between George IV Bridge and the Grassmarket in Edinburgh. Walkers add scale and life to your picture, but busy moments make a clean view tricky, so take a few frames. Keep it simple and choose one or two strong details rather than trying to fit everything in.

card.hook: You're standing on a drained loch, and now it's lawns, flower beds and a fountain with a castle looming over the top. Not a bad swap.
card.stand_here: In West Princes Street Gardens, stand about 75 m south of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. The fountain area is about 77 m ahead of you, roughly a minute's walk, with open lawn and path in front.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of the fountain and its surroundings. Try 0.5x if you want more lawn and trees, but keep the fountain away from the edges, where it can look stretched. Zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) is good for fountain details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the fountain on one of the vertical lines instead of dead centre, then tap the fountain and slide a bit darker if the sky or water looks washed out.
card.best_time: Early in the day usually means fewer people on the paths. Soft morning or late-afternoon light tends to flatter the water and flower beds, while midday sun can be harsh.
card.selfie_here: Stand in front of the Ross Fountain's basin with the castle rising behind you, from the south side of the gardens, which is the classic castle-backdrop frame. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more in, and keep the castle over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the grass just beneath the trees beside the fountain, and have them step back until the whole fountain fits, while you stand in front of the basin.
card.rules_and_safety: The gardens are a public park, but events and works can affect parts of them, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot, then walk a few paces closer and take a second. Can you spot which one has fewer bins and signs sneaking in at the edges?
card.good_to_know: The gardens sit on the old Nor Loch, which was drained before they were laid out in the 1820s. The West Gardens became a public park in 1876 and cover about 29 acres (12 ha). While you're here, look for the Ross Bandstand (1935) and the listed shelters on the upper walkway (1950).

card.hook: Picture a little cobbled lane that bends just enough to make you say "ooh", with a church clock tower waiting at the far end. That's Circus Lane, and yes, it's as postcard-pretty as it looks.
card.stand_here: Stand about 55 m south of the subject, on North West Circus Place (the phone icon on the map), and face north. Head to the end where the lane opens out, then turn back along the curve towards St Stephen's church.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the classic view along the curve. Try 2x if your phone has it for a second version, and use 0.5x only for a low shot of the cobbles and flowers, because it makes the tower look small.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the curve of the lane on one side and the clock tower near the top third line, and keep your phone level so the houses stand up straight.
card.best_time: Early morning, around 7am to 9am, is the quietest time. It's a narrow lane where people live, so even then it's hard to keep everyone out of the frame.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie on the bend in Circus Lane, where St Stephen's clock tower shows above the rooftops behind you. Use the front camera, hold it a little low and let the tower peek over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to someone on North West Circus Place and ask them to frame you in the lane, with the curve, cobbles and church behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: People live here, so keep your voice down and be discreet around windows and doors. Don't photograph through windows or block doorways. Cars can drive down the lane, so step onto the pavement when one comes past.
card.challenge: Get the clock tower in the top third of your shot with cobbles and flowers filling the bottom, then see if you can do it without a single stranger in the frame.
card.good_to_know: Circus Lane is a narrow, cobbled residential lane lined with mews houses, flowers and climbing greenery. A walking guide calls the view from the North West Circus Place end the most recognisable one, while another guide prefers the Stockbridge side, so both ends are worth a look. It's an open public street with no charge to view it.

card.hook: From the outside, Dynamic Earth looks less like a science centre and more like a giant pale tent that's pitched itself beside the Scottish Parliament. Behind it, the rough rock of Salisbury Crags makes the soft roof look even softer.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the phone icon on the map, at Dynamic Earth itself in Holyrood. Face the front of the building so the roof fills the view in front of you.
card.zoom: The building is about 94 m across, so start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole roof in. Then switch to 1x for a more natural look, and try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the masts, cables and the old brewery wall.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the main roof line on the lower third, and leave room above for sky and the hillside.
card.best_time: Early or late in the day gives soft light that flatters the pale roof. An overcast sky works well too, because the fabric keeps its detail. Try to skip harsh midday sun, which can wash the roof out.
card.selfie_here: Try the steps of the outdoor amphitheatre at the front, near the entrance. It's a popular spot on sunny days, and the front is the more-photographed side of the building. Use the front camera at 0.5x and tilt it up so the roof peeks over your shoulder. We couldn't confirm anyone has a perfect selfie there, so take a few and pick the best.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to shoot from the amphitheatre at the front, where the white roof and entrance both fit in the frame, while you pose in front of the building.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally allowed for personal use in most areas, but check for restrictions, especially in the planetarium during shows. If you plan to walk the Radical Road under the Crags, check its status first, as it was reported closed after a rockfall.
card.challenge: Hunt down the surviving section of the old Abbey Brewery wall and snap it at 2x, then see if a friend can spot it in your photo.
card.good_to_know: Dynamic Earth was designed by Michael Hopkins and Partners, opened in 1999, and won a RIBA Regional Award in 2001. The site was once a gasworks and part of the old Holyrood Brewery. The design keeps part of the original Abbey Brewery wall. You don't need to go inside to photograph the outside.

card.hook: Picture a calm, formal church front tucked among the old buildings of the Canongate, the kind of place that looks like it's been waiting for its photo. It has had a famous one before: Zara Phillips and Mike Tindall married here on 30 July 2011.
card.stand_here: Stand about 25 m south-east of Canongate Kirk, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west. The church is about 47 m across, so that bit of distance is what lets you fit the whole front in.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of the front. If the whole building won't fit, drop to 0.5x, and use 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the coat of arms and other details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the church's vertical edges with them so the building doesn't lean.
card.best_time: An overcast day gives soft, even light that suits the stonework. Early morning is usually quieter on the street, too.
card.selfie_here: Stand beside the bronze statue of the poet Robert Fergusson on the kirk grounds, on the Canongate side of the Royal Mile, then use the front camera at 0.5x and angle yourself so the kirk sits over your shoulder. In early May, the cherry trees in front of the kirk are in bloom and make a pretty frame.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by near the seating area in front of the kirk, opposite Crichton's Close, to take your photo with the church front behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working church, so be considerate of anyone going in or out, and check the official site for visiting times. Photos in the kirkyard are generally fine for personal use, but respect any services or events.
card.challenge: Find the Moodie coat of arms on the front and get a close-up of it before anyone else in your group spots it.
card.good_to_know: The kirk was finished in 1691 and designed by James Smith, after the congregation had to leave Holyrood Abbey. The arms of Thomas Moodie, whose bequest helped pay for it, are on the facade. Its parish takes in the Palace of Holyroodhouse and the Scottish Parliament, and it is also the parish church of Edinburgh Castle.

card.hook: Queen Mary's Bath House is only about 22 metres from the phone icon, so this one's a quick stop. You'll be done before your coffee cools.
card.stand_here: Stand about 20 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east towards Queen Mary's Bath House. It's a few seconds on foot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so you get the whole building with a little of its surroundings. Then try zoom 2x for details. Use zoom 0.5x only if you want even more of the setting, and keep the building away from the edges so it doesn't stretch.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines in your camera settings and line up the building's edges with the vertical lines so it doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people. You can photograph the building at any time of day, though.
card.selfie_here: Try the Abbeyhill pavement, at the railings where the information board stands, with the building behind you. Use the front camera, switch to zoom 0.5x if you want more in the shot, and keep the house over your shoulder. Photographers have shot the building from the Abbeyhill side, so treat this as a suggestion rather than an official selfie spot.
card.ask_someone: Stand on the road at Abbeyhill and ask someone to photograph you from the building's north-west front, where the house shows in full.
card.rules_and_safety: We have no access details for the building itself, so check the official site before you go and respect any signs or barriers.
card.challenge: Take one upright photo and one landscape photo, then pick the winner later.
card.good_to_know: Queen Mary's Bath House is on the Edinburgh map. We can only promise you its name and location, so we've left the history out. If you spot a sign or information board nearby, snap it as a handy reminder for later.

card.hook: Every line on this staircase points the same way: the step edges, the walls, the railings. All you have to do is point your phone along them. Bonus points if a stranger wanders into the shot.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 15 m south of the Scotsman Steps, and face north. The stairway is then straight ahead of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a natural view. If the walls feel tight and you can't fit the whole flight in, tap 0.5x. If you want the steps to look closer, try 2x (higher zooms depend on your phone) and keep your arms steady.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, line the stairway up down the middle, then tap the steps and slide it a touch darker if the sky at the top is bright.
card.best_time: Early in the day is usually quieter, so you're more likely to get a clear view of the steps. Soft daylight also keeps the bright top and the shaded walls from clashing.
card.selfie_here: Stand in the arched stone gateway with the wrought-iron gates at the North Bridge end, so the stair drops away behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to squeeze in more of the steps, and hold the phone upright.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on Market Street, on the street opposite the Fruitmarket Gallery where the stair lands near Waverley Station, to take your photo with the stairway behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The steps have gates that are closed at night to protect them, so photos after dark may not be possible. Check the official site or local signs for closures or works, and stay to the side so you don't block anyone.
card.challenge: Take five quick shots while people pass, then keep the one where the gap or the figure on the steps looks just right.
card.good_to_know: The walls close in around the steps, which gives the view an enclosed, slightly dramatic feel. A person walking up or down adds scale and a sense of life. For history and background, check a local guide or the city's official visitor pages.

card.hook: Forget columns and domes. This parliament is all angled walls, big windows and leaf-shaped shapes, low and spread out like it grew out of the hillside. That's exactly why it's fun to photograph.
card.stand_here: Stand about 65 m west of the Scottish Parliament Building, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. From here you can take in the whole group of buildings at once.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a natural view. Switch to 0.5x when you want the whole low, spreading complex in one frame. Then walk closer and try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for windows, roof shapes and textures.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the building, then slide the picture a touch darker if the sky is bright, so the stone and wood keep their texture.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light brings out the textures. A bright, even overcast day works well too, because it avoids harsh shadows across the walls.
card.selfie_here: Try the rear of the Parliament building, standing in front of its quirky windows. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and let the window patterns fill the space behind your shoulder. One older blog recommends this spot and mentions new concrete walls and spikes around the back, so check what's there when you arrive.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on the park paths at the back of the building to frame you with the angular roofs against Salisbury Crags, and check the exact spot on the map.
card.rules_and_safety: Personal photography is allowed in public areas of the Parliament, but not in the Debating Chamber or committee rooms during proceedings. It's a working parliament, so some areas may be restricted; check the official site before you go. The northern section of the Radical Road beneath Salisbury Crags is closed and fenced off, and only the southern stretch from the Hawse to the South Quarry is open.
card.challenge: Hunt down a leaf-shaped motif and take a close-up of it, then see if a friend can guess where it is.
card.good_to_know: Construction began in June 1999, and MSPs held their first debate here on 7 September 2004. Queen Elizabeth II formally opened it on 9 October 2004, and it won the Stirling Prize in 2005. Inside, the original lintel from Parliament House, where Scotland's old Parliament met until 1707, sits above the debating chamber.
